verifier_role: independent second agent; own synthetic staged bundles and export; the worker's fixtures and helpers were not imported
summary: The drvfs fallback meets all three acceptance items on this host. On both the Linux tmp path and /mnt/s, an existing destination is never overwritten. An interrupted or failed publish leaves either nothing or a directory marked RELEASE_INCOMPLETE.txt; in one rollback-failure case it leaves an empty unmarked directory. The atomic rename path is still the one used on Linux filesystems. Two low-severity hardening gaps were found and pinned as strict xfails (V1, V2). Neither affects the acceptance items. Done covers publication mechanics on fixtures only; it authorizes no release.

acceptance.item: Existing destination never overwritten on either filesystem
acceptance.evidence: On both filesystems: an existing empty directory, a directory with files, a plain file, a directory with a leftover marker, and a symlink to a directory are all refused, and their contents are untouched. A directory created between the rename failure and the mkdir gives FileExistsError, and the foreign file is untouched. A file or symlink planted at a later target name mid-publish is kept, and the symlink's target is untouched. EEXIST propagates and is never treated as an unsupported-link errno.

acceptance.item: Interrupted publish leaves no partial bundle or a clearly marked incomplete one
acceptance.evidence: A staged file mutated after hard-linking (same inode) is caught by the final hash check and rolled back. If a rollback unlink fails, the marker stays. If a rollback rmdir fails, only an empty unmarked directory is left, with nothing loadable. A subprocess killed during final verification, after every file including both manifest files was placed, leaves the marker. In that state every hash verifies, so the marker is the only sign the run did not finish; the DATA_CONTRACT paragraph tells readers to treat a marked directory as unusable. No tool in contributor_tools, docs or src reads release bundles, so no code reader needs a marker check yet.
Synthetic text artifacts and a two-observation synthetic export only. Temporary directories under /mnt/s/workspace (prefix .core05-verify-) were removed; ls shows no residue.

checks.evidence: git diff of build_dataset_release.py: the CORE-02 edits are intact (hash before admission; Arrow table kept; table.take positions; filtered_rows from num_rows). The new code splits _publish_directory into _rename_noreplace plus the fallback (_publish_files_exclusively, _place_exclusively, the INCOMPLETE_MARKER and errno sets), with docstring and comment updates. The one other behavioural change: a libc without renameat2 now raises ENOSYS and falls back, where it used to raise ReleaseError (stated in the handoff). File SHA-256 values match the worker handoff (builder 379b806a..., worker tests 41c3fd79...).

checks.area: fallback cannot trigger on Linux filesystems
checks.evidence: A full build on the ext4 tmp path succeeds with _publish_files_exclusively replaced by an assertion. On drvfs a full build goes through the fallback exactly once, ends unmarked and sealed, and leaves no staging or lock entries. Rename errors EEXIST, EACCES, EXDEV and ENOTEMPTY propagate without fallback on both filesystems. Only EINVAL, ENOSYS and EOPNOTSUPP trigger it, and stage and destination are siblings, so EINVAL cannot mean self-nesting. The drvfs rename probe (round 1 G1) still gives EINVAL for a new destination and EEXIST for an existing one.

On both filesystems a held .rel.release.lock refuses the build and is left intact, and no destination is created. O_EXCL is honoured on drvfs. After a hard kill the lock remains by design; the DATA_CONTRACT paragraph says to delete the marked directory and the lock by hand.

The CORE-05 paragraph sits in 'Release creation' after the overwrite sentence, and nothing else in that section changed. Its claims match the code: marker first, hard link or exclusive copy, manifest files last, hash check, marker removed last, rollback, and marker plus lock left after a hard interruption. Notes: (a) a libc without renameat2 also triggers the fallback; the docstring says so, the paragraph does not. (b) After an error with foreign entries, the marker stays but the lock is released; the 'treat any marked directory as unusable' rule still covers this. Other uncommitted hunks in DATA_CONTRACT.md (signs and frames, ensemble clocks, missing-value identity tokens, time_lineage) are not about publication. The sign text matches what the DOC-02/DOC-03 handoffs describe. Git cannot attribute uncommitted hunks, so 'CORE-05 added only this paragraph' rests on content, not history.

gaps.gap: After publication the fallback calls shutil.rmtree(stage, ignore_errors=True). If that cleanup fails (on drvfs, for example a Windows process holding a handle), the leftover .<name>.staging-* names are hard links to the published files. An edit to that residue changes the published release, and its manifest no longer verifies (shown on both filesystems). Between marker removal and rmtree the same aliasing exists briefly. The atomic rename path has no residue.
gaps.follow_up: Before removing the marker, unlink each staged name (move semantics) and roll back if any unlink fails; or confirm the stage is gone and report the residue. Then remove the strict-xfail marker on test_left_over_staging_names_cannot_change_a_published_release.

gaps.gap: The guard 'A staged release must contain only regular files' uses Path.is_file(), which follows symlinks, and os.link follows symlinks by default. A symlink planted in the staging directory (mkdtemp, owner-only) is published as a hard link to the outside file.
gaps.follow_up: Reject is_symlink() entries in the guard (or use lstat), then remove the strict-xfail marker on test_staged_symlink_is_refused_as_not_a_regular_file.

gaps.gap: If rmdir fails during rollback after the marker was removed, an empty unmarked destination remains. It holds nothing loadable and blocks a rebuild until removed.
gaps.follow_up: None required; optionally remove the marker only after rmdir succeeds.
